confounds: Strong activity-volume imbalance across all four folds can produce user-prevalence and raw-frequency artifacts.
The approximately 10:1 control-to-diagnosed class imbalance affects apparent predictive value and calibration.
Explicit mental-health language may be a collection or annotation artifact rather than a causal symptom signal.
No metadata were provided to separate demographic, age, community, fandom, political, or platform-composition effects from linguistic divergence.
Source order permits crude persistence checks but provides no dates, so temporary distress cannot be separated from long-term course.
Portuguese slang, spelling variation, sarcasm, lyrics, fiction, quotation, and conversational ellipsis make lexical context classification error-prone.
Bereavement, physical illness, relationship disruption, academic/work stress, and advocacy are plausible non-depression explanations for many enriched signals.

caveats: Could reflect collection, platform behavior, or label-associated sampling rather than depression.

findings.evidence_summary: Activity volume diverged consistently across folds, so user prevalence and normalized rates should be preferred over pooled post counts.
findings.prompt_guidance: Cap or match timeline length; report user-level prevalence and within-user post rates separately; do not let prolific users dominate.

negative_results: Bare negative-affect, sleep, isolation, work, romance, and illness terms are near-universal and have weak specificity.
Raw keyword counts are misleading: explicit depression appears in 0.094% of diagnosed posts versus 0.092% of control posts despite a much larger user-prevalence gap.
Literal suicidality is rare; death, killing, and mortality language is often figurative, fictional, quoted, or anger-related.

Absence is not strong counterevidence: 73.5% of diagnosed users lack any depression-word occurrence, 43.2% lack a high-confidence self-attributed mental-health mention, and 89.3% lack literal suicide-language occurrences.
Explicit denials are rare in both groups, so denial alone should not be treated as a reliable control signal.
